To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) there is high intrinsic variability in soft tissue mass and growth rate of freshwater mussels; (2) shell dimensions (particularly length) are poor predictors of soft tissue mass; and (3) the magnitude of variability in shell dimensions and soft tissue mass will influence the ability to detect effects in experimental studies of sublethally stressed mussels.

the coefficient of variation (a measure of the magnitude of variation in data) in shell length of Lampsilis was 0.66, the coefficient of variation of mussel soft tissue mass was 0.60, and the 95% credible interval of the relationship between mussel width and soft tissue mass was ∼145 mg. Intrinsic variability in

1) the coefficient of variation of L. sliquoidea soft tissues was less than the coefficient of variation for linear shell dimensions and 2) the 95% credible interval on soft tissue mass at any particular size class is about 145 mg.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the magnitude of variation in the size of L. sliquoidea, a commonly propagated species.
how to best estimate the size and growth rate in a population of L. silyquoidea.
how to best estimate mussel size and growth in the face of intrinsic variability.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the intrinsic variability of Lampsilis spp. soft tissues is high and should be considered when designing experiments and interpreting data.
the variability of shell growth is high and that the variability of soft tissue growth is lower but still high.
L. siliquoi-dea is a highly variable species with a large coefficient of variation for shell dimensions and a smaller CV for soft tissue growth.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the variability of shell and soft tissue growth is high, but that variability in shell dimensions is higher than variability in soft tissue mass.

the variability in shell dimensions of mussels is large enough to preclude using them as a response variable to detect small effects in sublethal stressor studies, but the soft tissue variability is low enough to make it a viable response variable in studies where the goal is to identify the magnitude of effects on metabolic rates.
variability in mussel soft tissues is high and the use of shell dimensions as predictors of soft tissue mass may not always be appropriate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
high intrinsic variability is common in unionids and that this must be considered when designing experiments or evaluating the success of restoration efforts.
high intrinsic variability in mussel shell and soft tissue size and growth rate will influence the interpretation and design of studies of unionids and their ecosystems.
the intrinsic variability of mussels is high.
